newsitem.title: USA: U.S. students score higher on college entrance exam.
newsitem.headline: U.S. students score higher on college entrance exam.

text.p: College-bound students scored higher on a widely used entrance exam for the second year in a row and the fourth time in five years, reflecting tougher classes in high school, test officials said Wednesday.
High school seniors scored an average of 21.0 on the 36-point American College Testing Program's ACT test, up from 20.9 last year and 20.6 in 1992.
"An increase in four out of five years definitely is a positive trend," ACT President Richard Ferguson said, adding that similar gains were made between 1984 and 1988.
Ferguson attributed the slightly increasing scores to greater numbers of high school students, especially minorities and females, taking higher-level college preparatory courses.

"This period of stable or increasing scores coincides almost exactly with a nationwide effort, beginning in about 1983, to improve the education we offer our young people, with a special emphasis on the need for more rigorous college-preparatory work," Ferguson said.
This year's score on the math section of the four-part ACT rose the most, by 0.4 points, which might have been because students were allowed to use calculators for the first time.
Male test-takers scored slightly higher than females, although the 0.2-point gender gap was as narrow as it has ever been and girls outperformed boys on the test's reading section.
The ACT exam is taken by nearly three out of five students heading to college.
